interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the flow lighting only along a path open all the way through a running pump, and going dark when one valve on it shuts, when you tap valves and pumps.
interactive.title: The cooling loop
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: Fifteen small screens. Some show an idea, and the rest ask you to try it. The main picture is a cooling water loop, drawn as a piping diagram. A small legend sits in one corner. Two centrifugal pumps, P1 and P2, sit side by side in parallel. Each is drawn as a circle with its outlet marked. Before each pump is its suction valve, V1 for P1 and V3 for P2. After each pump comes a non-return valve, NR1 and NR2. A small arrow shows the one way it passes. Then comes a discharge valve, V2 and V4. The two branches join and run to TV1, a three-way valve. One of its outlets runs through V7, the cooler HX1 and V8. The other is a bypass round the cooler. The two meet again and pass a small circle on the line. That is a temperature sensor, drawn as a plain circle with no letters. Then the line runs through the equipment the loop cools. A thin dashed line runs from the sensor to TV1. It carries a signal, not water. The water then comes back past the line from the header tank HT1. The tank keeps the loop full and gives the water room to expand. The water runs on through V5 and the strainer S1, and splits to the two pumps' suctions. Arrows on the lines show which way the water runs. Each part is named by its tag. The legend shows an open valve drawn hollow and a shut one filled in. Under the loop, Note 1 says TV1 is drawn in its fail position. The rule. In a pumped system like this, water flows only along a path open all the way through a running pump. The path runs from where the pump draws, through the pump, to where the water goes. In this closed loop, the water goes round and back to the pump's own suction. A line carrying flow is bold with arrows. A line with none is pale. A non-return valve passes water only its arrow's way. A stopped pump does not push. But water could pass through its casing. A running pump's discharge sits at a higher pressure than the suction. So only the stopped pump's non-return valve stops water running back through it. TV1 has three settings: through the cooler, some each way, or full bypass. In each, at least one of its outlets is open. If no open path runs from a running pump back to its suction, nothing flows. The pump is then marked running against a shut valve. The header tank's line never lights. It is joined to the loop but carries no flow. Tap a valve to open or shut it. Tap a pump to start or stop it. Tap TV1 to step its setting. The sheet opens on its drawn state. Every valve is open, and TV1 is set through the cooler. The running and stopped labels under the pumps show the plant now, not the drawing. P1 is running and P2 is stopped. On screens 4 and 6, a soft ring marks the part to tap until it is tapped. A line under the sheet says what the running pump is doing: pushing water round, or running against a shut valve. An Isolate switch changes what a tap does. Pick a part, then tap valves to shut them. Each pipe leaving the part shows red as far as the first valve on it, while that valve is open. A non-return valve counts as open here. It can let water back past its seat, and it cannot be locked shut. A stopped pump counts as open, because water passes through its casing. When no red pipe is left, the sheet says the part is cut off on every side. For a pump, it also says to lock off its starter. A Plant switch shows the loop as built, beside the drawing. It is a simple sketch, with the pipes running where they really go. Each valve has its tag plate. The sketch has one valve more than the drawing. That valve has no tag, sits on the line from the header tank, and is drawn shut. A Fuel tab picks a second sheet, a fuel transfer system. Storage tank 1's outlet valve F1 feeds a line through the strainer S2 to the transfer pump P3. From P3 the line runs through its non-return valve NR3 and the valve F3 into the day tank. Storage tank 2's outlet valve F2 feeds a second line. It joins tank 1's line before S2, through X1. X1 is a cross-connection, drawn shut. The same flow and isolate rules apply. Fuel runs from an open storage tank to the day tank. At phone width the loop is laid out tall rather than wide. Each tag sits beside its part, clear of the lines. The tabs and switches wrap onto two rows, with no word split. Every label is at least 12 px and readable at 360 px. Screen by screen. Screen 1, do, typed, Valve shut: the earlier pump's curve, head against flow, with no loop yet. "This pump's head is 30 − 0.04q² metres, where q is its flow in L/s. With its discharge valve open, it settled at 22 m. Shut that valve fully while it runs. What head does it give now?" A typed answer: 30, in m, a whole number. Slips: 22, "That is where it settled with the valve open. With the valve shut, no water flows."; 0, "No water flows, but the pump still pushes. Its head is highest with the outlet shut." Hint: "With the valve shut, the flow q is zero." Why: no water can pass, so q is 0. And 30 − 0.04 × 0² is 30 m. The pump spins and pushes, but nothing flows. No path is open. A right answer says "Full head, no flow." After Check, the cooling loop appears. Screen 2, show, The job first: the loop as it opens. Words: "This is a cooling water loop. Either of two pumps can push fresh water through a cooler and the equipment it cools, and back. Read the job first. Then name the parts. Then read the state they are drawn in." The parts light in turn, each with its tag. Read: the loop is at rest, with every part named by its tag. Still: the end of the sweep. Screen 3, do, As drawn: the loop as it opens, nothing lit. "Every valve is drawn open. The labels under the pumps show the plant now. P1 is running and P2 is stopped. What is P2 doing?" Choices: Standing by, ready to start (right); Running, sharing the load; Isolated for work. Hint on Running: "P2's label says stopped. Only P1 is running." Hint on Isolated: "Its suction and discharge valves are drawn open, so it is not cut off." Why: the sheet draws each valve in its normal position, unless a note says otherwise. Both of P2's valves are open. So it can start at once if P1 stops. That is a standby pump. After Check, P2 is ringed. Screen 4, show, One open path: the loop as drawn. Words: "In a pumped loop like this, water flows only where a path is open all the way through a running pump. Here it runs from P1 through the cooler and the equipment, and back to P1's suction. Shut one valve on that path and nothing flows at all." Then "Tap V7 to shut it, then tap it again." A soft ring marks V7 until it is tapped. Read: P1 is running. Water is lit from P1 through NR1, V2, TV1, V7, the cooler, V8, the equipment, V5 and the strainer, and back to P1. With V7 shut, nothing is lit, and P1 runs against a shut valve. Still: V7 open, the path lit. Screen 5, do, Back through P2?: P1 running, P2 stopped, every valve open, P2's branch not yet lit or dark. "P1 runs. P2 is stopped, with both its valves open. Does water run back through P2 to the suction?" Choices: No, its non-return valve stops it (right); Yes, back through P2; No, because P2 is stopped. Hint on Yes: "Look at NR2's arrow. Which way does it let water pass?" Hint on No, because P2 is stopped: "A stopped pump does not push, but water can pass through its casing. What else is on its branch?" Why: water leaving P1 reaches the top of P2's branch at NR2. P1's discharge is at a higher pressure than the suction. So water would run back through P2 if it could. NR2 passes water only away from P2, so the branch stays still. Without it, some of P1's water would run back through P2 and miss the cooler. After Check, NR2 rings. Screen 6, show, Through or round: P1 running. Words: "TV1 is a three-way valve. It sends the water through the cooler, round it through the bypass, or some each way. A temperature sensor sets it along the dashed line. That line carries a signal, not water." Then "Tap TV1." A soft ring marks TV1 until it is tapped. Read: TV1 is at full bypass. The water is lit through the bypass, round the cooler, and the cooler's line is pale. Still: TV1 at full bypass. Screen 7, do, If the air fails: TV1 set some each way, nothing lit. "TV1 is set some each way. Its diaphragm is worked by air. If the air supply fails, where does TV1 go?" Choices: Through the cooler (right); To full bypass; You cannot tell from the drawing. Hint on full bypass: "Nothing in the symbol says which way air moves TV1. Read the note under the loop." Hint on cannot tell: "The symbol alone cannot tell you. But read the note under the loop." Why: a diaphragm symbol does not say whether air opens or shuts a valve. So the symbol alone cannot tell you where TV1 goes when its air fails. Note 1 can. It says TV1 is drawn in its fail position, and it is drawn through the cooler. A three-way valve is sometimes drawn where it fails to, not where it normally sits. So read the notes before you trust a three-way valve's drawn position. After Check, TV1 steps to through the cooler, the flow lights that way, and TV1 rings. Screen 8, show, Cut off on every side: Isolate on, P2 picked. Words: "To work on a part, cut it off on every side. Shut a valve on every pipe that reaches it. Then drain it and prove it at zero. In isolate mode, a pipe still open to the part shows red." Then "Tap P2 to pick it." Read: Isolate is on and P2 is picked. Its suction pipe is red to V3. Its discharge pipe is red through NR2 to V4. Still: P2 picked, nothing shut. Screen 9, do, Isolate P2: Isolate on and P2 picked, nothing shut. No pipe shows red until the first tap or the first Check, so he traces the pipes himself first. "P2's casing must be opened while P1 keeps running. Tap the valves you would shut, then Check." The answer: V3 and V4. Hint on V4 alone: "The suction pipe is still red. It reaches the loop through V3." Hint on V3 alone: "The red runs through NR2 to V4. A non-return valve can let water back past its seat, and it cannot be locked shut." Hint on any valve off P2's branch: "That valve is not on P2's branch. Shut only what reaches P2, so P1 keeps cooling." Hint otherwise: "Follow every pipe from P2 to its first valve." Why: P2 has two pipes: its suction through V3, and its discharge through NR2 to V4. Shut and lock both valves, and lock off P2's starter. Then drain the casing and prove it at zero. P1 keeps the loop running throughout. After Check, the sheet says cut off on every side. Screen 10, show, Drawing against plant: the drawing. Words: "A drawing is only as good as its match with the plant. Before you trust it for an isolation, check every valve on the plant against it." Then "Tap Plant." Read: the plant sketch sits beside the drawing. It is the same loop, with its pipes where they really run. Still: Plant on. Screen 11, do, One too many: Plant on. "The plant has one valve the drawing does not show. Tap it." The answer: the untagged valve on the header tank's line. Hint on a tagged valve: "That one is on the drawing. Look for a valve with no tag." Why: it sits on the header tank's line, and it is shut. It cuts the loop off from its header tank. The drawing gives no sign of it. As the water warms, it expands. With nowhere to go, the loop's pressure climbs. After Check, a dashed ghost of it appears on the drawing. Screen 12, show, A second path: the Fuel sheet. Words: "This sheet moves fuel from two storage tanks to a day tank. X1 is a cross-connection, drawn shut. It joins tank 2's line to the pump's suction. Open it, and P3 can draw from tank 2 as well." Then "Tap X1." Read: X1 is open and P3 is running. Fuel is lit from both tanks through S2, P3, NR3 and F3 into the day tank. Still: X1 open. Screen 13, do, mixed, Which tank?: the fuel sheet, P3 running, F1 shut, F2 and X1 open, nothing lit. "P3 runs. F1 is shut, and F2 and X1 are open. Where does P3 draw from?" Choices: Tank 2 only (right); Tank 1 only; Both tanks. Hint on Tank 1 only: "F1 is shut. Follow the line from tank 2 through X1." Hint on Both tanks: "F1 is shut, so tank 1's line stops there." Why: F1 shuts tank 1's line at the tank. Tank 2's fuel runs through F2 and the open X1 into the suction. Then it runs on through S2 and P3 to the day tank. After Check, that path lights. Screen 14, do, mixed, typed, Clean the strainer: the fuel sheet, X1 open, P3 stopped. "X1 is open, and P3 is stopped and locked off. You must open S2 to clean it. What is the smallest number of valves you must shut?" A typed answer: 3, no unit, a whole number. Slips: 1, "That cuts off one side only. S2 has pipes on both sides."; 2, "Count every pipe that reaches S2. X1 joins tank 2's line to it. And a non-return valve is not an isolation."; 4, "Shutting X1 already cuts off tank 2's line. F2 adds nothing." Hint: "Count every pipe that reaches S2, on both sides." Why: two lines reach S2 from before it. Tank 1's comes through F1, and tank 2's through X1. After S2, the line runs through the stopped P3 and NR3 to F3, with the day tank beyond. Shut F1, X1 and F3. After Check, the three valves ring. Screen 15, do, mixed, Gate or globe?: the fuel sheet as drawn. "F1 and F3 are drawn with the same valve symbol. On the plant, F1 is a gate valve and F3 a globe valve. Where would the drawing tell you that?" Choices: In each valve's tag or the sheet's notes and legend (right); In the valve symbol itself; Nowhere, so you must guess. Hint on the symbol: "Gate and globe valves are often drawn the same. F1 and F3 look alike here." Hint on guess: "Never guess what a valve is. Other parts of the drawing can say." Why: gate and globe valves are often drawn with the same symbol, so the symbol cannot tell them apart. The valve's tag or the sheet's notes and legend may say which it is. If nothing on the sheet says, check the valve on the plant. After Check, F1 and F3 ring.
interactive.ignores: Water and fuel are drawn as either flowing or still, with no pressures or flow rates on the lines. TV1's middle setting is drawn as some each way, with no share given. In the flow picture, a non-return valve holds perfectly and a shut valve seals perfectly. Real ones can let a little by. That is why isolate mode treats a non-return valve as open. The header tank's line is drawn with no flow. In fact, a little water moves in and out as the loop warms and cools. The plant view is a sketch, not a photograph. Nothing here flows without a running pump. On real plant, a higher tank or trapped pressure can push flow too. Real piping diagrams carry far more: line numbers, sizes, materials, vents, drains and many instruments. Nothing here shows how pipes, pumps or valves are sized.

explain.text:
On a pumped system, a pump drives flow only along a path that is open all the way through it. That path runs from where the pump draws, through the pump, to where the water goes. So to find the flow, read each valve's position and each pump's state, then trace. To work on a part safely, shut a valve on every pipe that reaches it.

Start with the job, then the parts. Here, either of two centrifugal pumps can push fresh water round a loop. It runs through a cooler and the equipment it cools, and back. Each pump has a suction valve before it. After it come a non-return valve and a discharge valve. A strainer on the common suction catches dirt. A header tank keeps the loop full and gives the water room to expand. Then read the drawn state. The sheet shows each valve in its normal position, unless it says otherwise.[^1] Here P1 runs. P2 is stopped with both its valves open. So P2 stands by, ready to start.

The positions of every valve at one time are the [[valve lineup]]. You trace from it. Water leaves P1 and goes through the cooler and the equipment. Then it comes back to P1's suction. Why does none run back through P2? P1's discharge sits at a higher pressure than the suction. So any open way between them would carry water back. A stopped pump does not push. But water can still pass through its casing. A [[non-return valve]] is built to pass water one way only. P2's non-return valve points away from the pump, so P2's branch stays still. Shut one valve on P1's path and nothing flows. The path is broken. A centrifugal pump then runs against the shut valve at full head, with no flow.

The three-way valve TV1 is different. It sends the water through the cooler, round it through a bypass, or some each way. It picks a path. So the water keeps moving, whichever way it is set.

To isolate a part, follow every pipe from it to its first valve, on both sides. Shut each of those valves. Pumps are not the only push. A higher tank or trapped pressure can push water too. So a part is safe only when every way in is shut. For P2, that is V3 on its suction and V4 on its discharge. NR2 is not enough. A non-return valve can let water back past its seat. And it cannot be locked shut.

A [[cross-connection]] is a valve that joins two lines which would otherwise be separate. On the fuel sheet, X1 joins tank 2's line to the pump's suction. When X1 is open, it adds a second path. So to isolate anything past it, you shut X1 too.

All this rests on the drawing matching the plant. Before you trust a drawing for an isolation, check on the plant each valve you will use. It must be there, where the drawing puts it.[^2] A valve on the plant that the drawing does not show can change the paths without warning.

Even a true drawing leaves things out. Gate and globe valves are often drawn with the same symbol.[^3] The valve's tag or the sheet's notes may say which it is. A diaphragm on a valve does not say whether air opens it or shuts it.[^4] And a three-way valve is sometimes drawn in the position it fails to, not its normal one.[^5] So read the notes. Here, Note 1 says TV1 is drawn in its fail position. When one sheet shows two systems of the same kind, extra letters on the symbols tell them apart.[^6]

**A pump drives flow only along paths open all the way through it. Other pressure can push too, so to isolate a part, shut a valve on every pipe that reaches it.**

analogy.text: You know this from isolating a motor starter with a separate control supply. Locking off the main breaker is not enough while the control circuit is fed from somewhere else. You open every supply that reaches it, then prove it dead. A part on a pipe is the same. Every pipe that reaches it is a way in. Each needs its own shut valve.
analogy.breaks: A shut valve leaves water and its pressure trapped inside the part. So you also drain or vent it, and prove it at zero. A shut valve can also leak past its seat. So you prove a pipe isolation by pressure, not with a tester at the terminals.

practice.text:
- Safety first. Stop and lock off any pump on the part. Shut and lock a valve on every pipe that reaches it. Never count a non-return valve as one. Then drain or vent the part and prove it at zero, by the plant's procedure.
- Read the job: what the system moves, and from where to where.
- Name the parts by their tags. Find the pumps and the tanks.
- Read the drawn state: each valve in its normal position, unless a note says otherwise.
- Set the lineup you have now. From each running pump, trace along open valves only, to where the water goes.
- To isolate a part, follow every pipe from it to its first valve, on both sides. Watch for bypasses and cross-connections. They add pipes.
- Check the drawing against the plant, valve by valve, before you trust it.

**Rule of thumb:** count the pipes that reach the part. Each one that leads anywhere needs a shut valve.

**Worked example:** the cooling loop. As drawn, P1 runs and P2 stands by with its valves open. Water runs from P1 through NR1 and V2 to TV1. Then it goes through the cooler, the equipment and the strainer, and back to P1. NR2 stops it running back through P2. To open P2's casing with P1 still running, first lock off P2's starter. Shut and lock V3 and V4. Then drain the casing and prove it at zero.

**Common mistakes**
- Reading a stopped pump as a shut path.
- Counting a non-return valve as an isolation.
- Reading a three-way valve as a shut-off.
- Shutting one side of a part and missing the other.
- Missing a bypass or cross-connection that adds a second path.
- Trusting the drawing without checking it against the plant.
- Telling a gate valve from a globe valve by its symbol alone.
- Taking a three-way valve's drawn position as normal without reading the notes.

sources.quote: Unless otherwise stated, P&IDs indicate valves in their "normal" position. This is usually interpreted as the normal or primary flowpath for the system. An exception is safety systems, which are normally shown in their standby or non-accident condition.

sources.title: The safe isolation of plant and equipment (HSG253)
sources.quote: Are all isolation points identified on the plant and do they match the line diagram and isolation certificate?

sources.quote: globe and gate valves will often be depicted by the same valve symbol. In such cases, information concerning the valve type may be conveyed by the component identification number or by the notes and legend section of the drawing
